--- title: "Lab 1: Simulation & Types of Data" subtitle: "FW 532 · Python version" --- **Goals:** * To get comfortable simulating data in Python. **You Will Need:** * The course environmental raster stack (`data/envStack.tif`, included in the starter kit) * Python packages: numpy, pandas, matplotlib, statsmodels, rasterio (see `requirements.txt`) * The course helper module `sdmlab.py` (in the same folder as this notebook) > **New to Python notebooks?** A notebook is a list of *cells*. Click a code cell and press > **Shift + Enter** to run it. Run the cells in order from top to bottom: later cells use > variables created by earlier ones. ::: {#e893ac90 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Running on Google Colab? This cell downloads the course files. (Anywhere else it does nothing.) import os, sys if "google.colab" in sys.modules: if not os.path.exists("/content/fw532"): !git clone -q --depth 1 https://github.com/Hutchinson-Lab/fw532.git /content/fw532 %pip install -q rasterio os.chdir("/content/fw532/python") ``` ::: First, load the packages we need. `sdmlab` is a small helper module written for this course. It does the raster (map) operations that the `terra` package does in the R version of the labs. Open `sdmlab.py` if you're curious -- it is ordinary numpy and matplotlib code. ::: {#c9d95035 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.api as sm import sdmlab as sdm # course helpers for rasters ``` ::: Here are a few environmental variables for us to start with. These are climatic variables from WorldClim (averages for 1970-2000; ) and elevation, covering roughly North America. The spatial resolution is 10 minutes, which is about 13km at 45 degrees latitude. More generally, you could start with any set of variables at any extent that you wish. A raster is a grid of cells. In Python we store it as a 2-D array (rows × columns); a *stack* of 20 rasters is a 3-D array (layers × rows × columns). Ocean cells have no data, which numpy writes as `nan` ("not a number"). ::: {#da00292b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} env_stack = sdm.load_env() print(env_stack) print(env_stack.values.shape) # (layers, rows, columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EnvStack size : 385 rows x 691 cols x 20 layers resolution : 0.166667 degrees extent : -167.6667, -52.5000, 7.1667, 71.3333 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) crs : EPSG:4326 layers : Annual.Mean.Temperature, Mean.Diurnal.Range, Isothermality, Temperature.Seasonality, Max.Temperature.of.Warmest.Month, Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month, Temperature.Annual.Range, Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter, Mean.Temperature.of.Driest.Quarter, Mean.Temperature.of.Warmest.Quarter, Mean.Temperature.of.Coldest.Quarter, Annual.Precipitation, Precipitation.of.Wettest.Month, Precipitation.of.Driest.Month, Precipitation.Seasonality, Precipitation.of.Wettest.Quarter, Precipitation.of.Driest.Quarter, Precipitation.of.Warmest.Quarter, Precipitation.of.Coldest.Quarter, elevation (20, 385, 691) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a4517b23 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} env_stack.plot(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1393 height=1040} ::: ::: # A data simulator Next, let's select some locations to simulate species data. Random numbers in Python come from a *random number generator*. If we create the generator with a fixed *seed* (any number), we all get the same "random" results, which makes the lab reproducible. You'll see a seed given every time we do something random. Let's scale the environmental variables, since we'll work with simple regression frameworks to start. ::: {#433d7d38 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # scale variables (each layer gets mean 0 and standard deviation 1) env_stack = env_stack.scale() n_points = 1000 # pick random land cells; could change this from random to a procedure reflecting sampling bias sim_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=1234) sim_pts.iloc[:5, :5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
x y Annual.Mean.Temperature Mean.Diurnal.Range Isothermality
0 -77.916667 48.583333 -0.228389 0.243981 -0.404329
1 -94.583333 17.083333 1.886109 -0.277266 1.893295
2 -93.916667 61.250000 -1.112822 -1.032349 -0.936383
3 -131.750000 68.750000 -1.106385 -0.604168 -0.813565
4 -91.083333 29.416667 1.576260 -0.316824 0.418138
``` ::: ::: `sim_pts` is a pandas DataFrame (a table) with one row per sampled location: the coordinates (`x` = longitude, `y` = latitude) followed by the value of each environmental layer at that location. ::: {#4c32c0c4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # plot the points over the first climate raster: ax = sdm.plot_map(env_stack["Annual.Mean.Temperature"], env_stack, title="Annual.Mean.Temperature") ax.scatter(sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"], s=4, color="black"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=529 height=293} ::: ::: To simulate a species, we'll make up a function to define its probability of occurrence as a function of the environmental variables. Let's look at their correlation as we consider what variables to include. ::: {#1af19937 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # check out their correlation (Spearman's rank correlation): correl = sim_pts[env_stack.names].corr(method="spearman") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8)) im = ax.imshow(correl, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1) ax.set_xticks(range(len(correl)), correl.columns, rotation=90, fontsize=8) ax.set_yticks(range(len(correl)), correl.index, fontsize=8) fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Spearman correlation"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=903 height=803} ::: ::: Somewhat arbitrarily, let's use variables 6, 15, and 8 (Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month, Precipitation.Seasonality, and Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter). The coefficients of the linear function are somewhat arbitrary as well ('hand-tuned'). Note that we're scaling the input variables as we compute this, so that every variable is on a comparable scale. Each `env_stack["..."]` below is a whole map (a 2-D array), so `p_occ` is computed for every cell at once. ::: {#97d152f7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def logistic(x): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x)) # parameters intercept = -1.5 beta1 = -1.5 beta2 = -1.5 beta3 = 1.5 p_occ = logistic(intercept + beta1 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Precipitation.Seasonality"]) + beta2 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month"]) + beta3 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"])) # plot the three relevant climate variables and the probability of occurrence fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5), constrained_layout=True) for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"]): sdm.plot_map(env_stack[name], env_stack, ax=ax, title=name) sdm.plot_map(p_occ, env_stack, ax=axes[1, 1], title="Probability of Occurrence"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1066 height=608} ::: ::: Next, we use `rng.binomial()` to "flip a coin" with probability of heads corresponding to the value of the `p_occ` surface at the sampling points. Points with a high p_occ (e.g., 0.9) will be more likely (but not certain) to be heads (present). Points with a low p_occ (e.g., 0.2) will be more likely (but not certain) to be tails (absent). ::: {#4cf438b2 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # get the values that correspond to the points we selected: probs = sdm.extract(p_occ, env_stack, sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"]) # sample from these probabilities (note the *different* seed -- see below): rng = np.random.default_rng(5678) obs = rng.binomial(n=1, p=probs) # put response and variables together in a DataFrame: modeling_df = sim_pts.copy() modeling_df.insert(0, "PresAbs", obs) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) for value, color in [(0, "tab:red"), (1, "tab:cyan")]: rows = modeling_df["PresAbs"] == value ax.scatter(modeling_df.loc[rows, "x"], modeling_df.loc[rows, "y"], s=6, color=color, label=str(value)) ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.legend(title="PresAbs"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=566 height=336} ::: ::: > **Why a different seed?** Fixing seeds makes results reproducible, but **don't reuse the same > seed for different steps**: you would replay the same stream of random numbers. In R, reusing > `set.seed(1234)` here makes the presence/absence coin-flips depend on the random numbers that chose > the locations, which correlates "present" with latitude and biases the fitted coefficients. Using a > new seed for each random step avoids that trap. Now, supposing we had only been given these data, we could imagine fitting a model to them. Let's start with logistic regression, using the `statsmodels` package. A logistic regression is a *generalized linear model* (GLM) with a binomial family -- the same thing R's `glm(..., family = "binomial")` fits. `sm.add_constant()` adds the intercept column. ::: {#3f59cafc .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} vars1 = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"] model1 = sm.GLM(modeling_df["PresAbs"], sm.add_constant(modeling_df[vars1]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() print(model1.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Generalized Linear Model Regression Results ============================================================================== Dep. Variable: PresAbs No. Observations: 1000 Model: GLM Df Residuals: 996 Model Family: Binomial Df Model: 3 Link Function: Logit Scale: 1.0000 Method: IRLS Log-Likelihood: -417.98 Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 Deviance: 835.97 Time: 21:59:20 Pearson chi2: 917. No. Iterations: 6 Pseudo R-squ. (CS): 0.2885 Covariance Type: nonrobust ======================================================================================================= coef std err z P>|z| [0.025 0.975] ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- const -1.6365 0.118 -13.904 0.000 -1.867 -1.406 Precipitation.Seasonality -1.6333 0.133 -12.301 0.000 -1.894 -1.373 Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month -1.6777 0.166 -10.131 0.000 -2.002 -1.353 Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter 1.6596 0.158 10.529 0.000 1.351 1.969 ======================================================================================================= ``` ::: ::: Notice that our parameter estimates are close to the true values we used to simulate the data, as you might expect. > **Question:** Under what conditions would you NOT expect the parameter estimates to be close to > the true values? Of course, we might not know the correct variables in advance! > **Question:** What happens if you omit one of the variables we used? What happens if you add some > variables that we didn't use? Here are some more concrete models for you to check out as you answer these questions (use `print(model2.summary())` and so on to inspect them): ::: {#620cd11c .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} def fit_logistic(variables, data=modeling_df): """Fit a logistic regression of PresAbs on the given variables.""" return sm.GLM(data["PresAbs"], sm.add_constant(data[variables]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() vars2 = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Mean.Temperature.of.Coldest.Quarter", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"] vars3 = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Temperature.Seasonality", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"] vars4 = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter", "Mean.Diurnal.Range"] model2 = fit_logistic(vars2) model3 = fit_logistic(vars3) model4 = fit_logistic(vars4) ``` ::: In addition to looking at the estimated parameters, we can look at the predicted maps from these models. To predict a map, we make a table with one row per land cell (`to_frame()`), predict for every row, and put the predictions back onto the grid (`to_map()`). ::: {#654ed8d1 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = env_stack.to_frame() # one row per land cell pred1 = env_stack.to_map(model1.predict(sm.add_constant(grid[vars1]))) pred2 = env_stack.to_map(model2.predict(sm.add_constant(grid[vars2]))) pred3 = env_stack.to_map(model3.predict(sm.add_constant(grid[vars3]))) pred4 = env_stack.to_map(model4.predict(sm.add_constant(grid[vars4]))) fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(14, 6), constrained_layout=True) maps = [p_occ, pred1, pred2, pred3, pred4] titles = ["Truth", "Model1", "Model2", "Model3", "Model4"] for ax, m, title in zip(axes.flat, maps, titles): sdm.plot_map(m, env_stack, ax=ax, title=title, vmin=0, vmax=1) axes[1, 2].set_visible(False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab01-simulation_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=1354 height=545} ::: ::: > **Exercise:** Create your own simulated species by modifying the code above in some way. If you > need inspiration, perhaps consider a species you are interested in. You could change the important > variables, the parameter values, the sampling procedure, the type of data that is created (e.g., > abundance instead of presence/absence; try `rng.poisson()`)... Have fun! # Turn in **(a Canvas discussion post, by the due date on Canvas)** Please post to the online discussion of this lab. Please include a brief description of your simulated species (what aspects of the process you explored), along with plots and any comments you have about the exercise. Please also include, if applicable: * Any key take-aways from this lab that you want to remember for any future projects you may conduct in which you use species distribution models. * Any remaining questions or confusions do you have that you might like to learn more about.
